extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, judges, and agency counsel litigating or advising on FOIA/APA disclosure and reverse-FOIA cases
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and stepwise framework for judicial review of agency decisions to disclose submitter-provided information under FOIA and agency disclosure regulations, including when de novo evidence is appropriate, remand versus trial de novo, and statutory limits on implied private causes of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosures pursuant to valid agency regulations are not subject to §1905
rubrics_metrics.description: “disclosures pursuant to validly adopted agency regulations are not subject to the strictures of § 1905.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court follows Westinghouse: if an agency validly promulgates disclosure regulations under an independent authorizing statute (e.g., §301), disclosures made pursuant to those regulations are “authorized by law” and therefore outside the prohibitions of 18 U.S.C. §1905. The opinion cites multiple agencies that have adopted such regulations and stresses that the 1958 amendment to §301 was intended to eliminate governmental secrecy, not to preclude rulemaking authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: §301 as separate source of authority for promulgating disclosure regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: “§301 is a separate source of agency authority for the promulgation of disclosure regulations, and disclosures pursuant to such regulations are authorized by law and immune from the prohibitions of §1905.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because §301 authorizes the Office of the Federal Contract Compliance (OFCC) and similar agencies to promulgate disclosure regulations, courts should treat disclosures made under those regulations as lawful. The court relies on legislative history and precedent (e.g., Non-Resident Taxpayers Ass’n) to support this conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper construction of the 1958 amendment to §301 (legislative history)
rubrics_metrics.description: The addition of the last sentence [to §301] was aimed at stopping agencies from relying on the housekeeping statute as authority to deny the requests of citizens for information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congressman Moss's statement that the amendment 'does not affect the confidential status of information given to the government . . . in §1905' does not mean the amendment eliminated longstanding disclosure authority; the 1958 amendment's central purpose was elimination of governmental secrecy, so it should not be read to transmogrify §1905 into a tool to block disclosures authorized by regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied private cause of action from criminal non-disclosure statutes is disfavored
rubrics_metrics.description: “Recent pronouncements of the Supreme Court have severely limited the circumstances in which a federal court may imply a private cause of action from a federal statute... we do not believe we can properly imply a cause of action, and thus the right to a trial de novo, from § 1905.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a statute is criminal and provides penalties (fines, imprisonment, removal), courts are reluctant to imply a private civil cause of action to enforce it; the availability of remedies under the APA and the risk of complex statutory construction counsels against implying such a private right.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and scope of 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-8(e) (Title VII §709(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: “By its terms §709(e) applies only to employees of EEOC, and only to information obtained by that agency on its own statutory authority.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary rules of statutory construction for criminal statutes weigh against applying §709(e) to officers or employees of other agencies or to information obtained by other agencies under their separate authority. Even if agencies perform similar functions, independent statutory authority and Congressional choices regarding agency structure (e.g., keeping OFCC functions separate from EEOC) are controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: JRC/Coordinating Council does not extend applicability of §709(e) to other agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: “Nothing in 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-14 or in the implementing regulations which created JRC suggests an intention to extend the applicability of §709(e) to federal employees outside EEOC or to information possessed by other agencies on their own authority.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Joint Reporting Committee is an inter-agency collection agent; its role in collecting and distributing EEO-1 forms for multiple agencies does not make those forms the exclusive province of EEOC for purposes of §709(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: 44 U.S.C. § 3508 governs inter-agency transfers and sets conditions for release
rubrics_metrics.description: Text of §3508: (a) officers/employees of receiving agency become subject to unlawful-disclosure provisions to same extent as original agency; (b) information obtained under the chapter may be released to another Federal agency only (1) as statistical totals or summaries; or (2) if not declared confidential at time of collection; or (3) with consent of persons supplying information; or (4) when the receiving agency has authority to collect the information itself and that authority is supported by criminal penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §3508 applies only to inter-agency transfers, not to agency disclosures to the general public. The clause in §3508(a) making receiving-agency employees subject to the original penalties applies only when the receiving agency ‘obtained’ the information from the original agency rather than having obtained it independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of APA judicial review for submitters of information
rubrics_metrics.description: “Judicial review pursuant to the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) is available because a submitter may be ‘[a] person suffering legal wrong because of agency action ... within the meaning of a relevant statute.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in reverse-FOIA situations, a submitter whose information the agency intends to disclose can obtain judicial review under the APA (5 U.S.C. §702); courts that previously denied such review have been overruled or distinguished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary scope of judicial review under the APA — record review
rubrics_metrics.description: “Judicial review under the APA ordinarily is limited to a ‘review of the whole [agency] record or parts of it cited by a party.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewing court generally confines itself to the agency record; taking live testimony to decide the merits is not the norm. Evidence may be taken for interim relief under §705, and there are limited exceptions for de novo review described below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions permitting de novo review
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has approved de novo rather than agency record review (a) when the agency’s action is either adjudicatory in nature and its factfinding procedures are inadequate, or (b) when issues that were not before the agency are raised in a proceeding to enforce nonadjudicatory agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before conducting a trial de novo, a court should first decide whether the agency’s action was adjudicatory and whether its procedures were adequate. The district court erred by relying on trial testimony to decide the substantive merits without addressing that threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-step analysis framework for reverse FOIA cases
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Inquire whether any non-disclosure statute or non-disclosure regulation is applicable — if so, conclude agency acted outside statutory authority and enjoin disclosure. 2) If not, determine under what authority the agency intends to disclose the contested information. 3) If the agency says FOIA mandates disclosure, examine whether the agency applied the proper legal standards for the applicability of the FOIA exemptions. 4) If the agency says the information is within an exemption but disclosure is nevertheless permitted under the agency’s own disclosure regulations, first examine whether the agency applied proper FOIA exemption standards and then examine whether the agency considered the proper factors in determining that disclosure was permitted under its own regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: under OFCC disclosure regulations the agency may disclose only if it determines disclosure would ‘further the public interest and [not] impede the discharge of any of the functions of the OFCC or the Compliance Agencies.’ Where the record does not permit the court to perform these analyses, remand to the agency is the appropriate remedy; interim relief may be granted under 5 U.S.C. §705.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step test when agency relies on its own disclosure regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: When an agency concludes information falls within a FOIA exemption but nonetheless discloses under its own disclosure regulations, the reviewing court must (a) examine whether the agency applied proper legal standards for FOIA exemptions, and if so (b) examine whether the agency considered the proper factors in determining that disclosure was permitted under its own disclosure regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency record must state that disclosure is in the public interest and explain why (or, where FOIA mandates disclosure, why exemptions do not apply). Absent such an explanation, remand is required for additional agency findings or explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remand (not trial de novo) is the proper remedy for an inadequate administrative record
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the agency record does not establish, or insufficiently explains, the basis for the agency’s decision, so as not to permit the reviewing court to effectively perform the above analysis, the remedy is not a trial de novo, but a remand to the agency for an additional record or explanation for its decision.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Camp v. Pitts permits supplementation by affidavits/testimony in limited circumstances, but where the record is ambiguous as to the basis for disclosure the appropriate course is remand. The district court’s use of trial testimony to decide merits was improper where no threshold finding on adjudicatory character was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion and meaningful-timing principle for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: “Judicial review of agency action must be available at a meaningful time considering the nature of the alleged injury to the petitioner for review.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an agency regards the FOIA 10-day limit as binding and disclosure would render judicial review moot, courts should not allow an internal administrative appeal procedure to destroy the subject matter of a judicial proceeding. Exhaustion of an optional regulatory administrative appeal should not foreclose timely judicial review when meaningful judicial relief would otherwise be lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural due process standard for pre-disclosure process
rubrics_metrics.description: “To the extent that Chrysler's due process claims are procedural we hold that... OFCC disclosure regulation 41 C.F.R. § 60-60.4(d), coupled with the process of administrative and judicial review set out above in Part IVC, meet fifth amendment due process standards.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court rejects the claim that predisclosure notice and hearing are constitutionally required beyond the administrative and judicial review procedures established; substantive due process claims asserting proprietary interests in information are speculative and not resolved absent a final release decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiff's burden in reverse-FOIA cases to prove applicability of a FOIA exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: “The FOIA requires the Plaintiff in this ‘reverse’ Freedom of Information case to prove that the information requested is not in the category of information which must be disclosed upon request. To do this, Plaintiff must prove that the information sought by the requestor is within one of the nine categories of information excepted from mandatory disclosure in 5 U.S.C. § 552(b).”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plaintiff must identify which exemption(s) apply and produce an agency record basis supporting that claim. In this case the court found the plaintiff failed to show any category other than §552(b)(4) applied, and that (b)(4) only covered the manning tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: 29 C.F.R. §70.21(a) and other agency regs prohibit only disclosures 'not authorized by law'
rubrics_metrics.description: 29 C.F.R. § 70.21(a), modeled after 18 U.S.C. §1905, only prohibits disclosures 'not authorized by law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosures are authorized by law (e.g., made pursuant to valid OFCC disclosure regulations under §301), those regulatory prohibitions do not apply. Courts should compare the agency regulation's language to statutory provisions to determine whether the agency acted 'in accordance with law.'
